summary: Son of a Palatine immigrant at Easton who settled about 1800 on the Susquehanna flats at Hunlock's Creek and owned "Stewart's Flats" in Plymouth; John's 5th-great-grandfather.
bio:
Frederick Croup, whose name was written Grub, Croop, Krub, Grupe and Crapp in different records, was born about 1767 in Northampton County, Pennsylvania, a son of Andreas Grub, a Palatine immigrant at Easton. He was confirmed at St. John's Lutheran Church in Easton in 1783, aged 15. When his father died in 1791, Frederick and his mother were the executors of the will, and he inherited jointly with his brother John; he was still in Forks Township in 1800, and his mother's will of 1810 names "her son Frederick Krub".

About 1800 he moved to Luzerne County and, as a county history put it, "settled near the river and opened the I. Davenport farm" at the mouth of Hunlock's Creek, while John Croop and the Sorbers settled further up the creek and built the sawmills. His daughter Susan was born at Nanticoke in May 1800. Frederick himself was a farmer and landowner near the river rather than a mill man; the Croop mills and the later Croop's Glen amusement park belonged to his nephew John Croop's line. A captive's narrative published in 1833 recalls that Indians killed Asa Upson on 28 March 1780 at "Stewart's Flats, now owned by Frederick Croup, in Plymouth", and the "Dutch Fishery" shad haul below Nanticoke used "the upper end of the Croup farm" as its landing; the owner was probably this Frederick. In 1812 his brother Philip's will named "my dear brother Frederick Grupe" as co-executor. A "gentleman named Croup" was jailed by Judge Thomas Cooper, together with the Kingston constable Stephen Hollister, for whispering in court, one of the charges that led to Cooper's removal in 1811, but which Croup that was is not known.

He married Mary Young, and the Harvey family history records "Frederick and Mary (Young) Croup" as the parents of Susan Croup Shupp. His known children were Susan (1800-1863), who married Philip Shupp Jr., and Elizabeth (1802-1895), who married James Pringle; other lists name Sarah, Mary, Margaret, Catherine, William, Peter, John and Ann. In 1820 he headed a large household in Plymouth that included two young men, two girls aged 10 to 15 and a young woman, and in 1840, a man in his seventies with a wife in her sixties, he was still in Plymouth Township with a younger couple, probably a married child, living with them. He died in Luzerne County in 1841, before 10 April, and his will was recorded in the county that year; Mary is said to have died the same year. He is John's 5th-great-grandfather.
funFacts: His farm at Stewart's Flats was the site of the 1780 killing of Asa Upson in an Indian raid.
His farm was the landing for the 'Dutch Fishery' shad haul at the Nanticoke narrows.

researchNotes:
Frederick Grub was confirmed at St. John's Lutheran, Easton, in 1783 aged 15 as a son of Andreas Grub, placing his birth about 1767-68 (tree: no birth date, d. 1841). He and his mother were executors of his father's 1791 will; he was in Forks Twp in the 1800 census and co-executor with his mother in an Aug 1800 Northampton deed, and inherited jointly with his brother John. His mother's 1810 will names 'her son Frederick Krub'. About 1799-1800 he moved to Luzerne County: Bradsby says that 'soon after' about 1790 'Fredrick Croop settled near the river and opened the I. Davenport farm' at the mouth of Hunlock's Creek, while John Croop and the Sorbers settled further up the creek, and the 'Sorbers and Croops were mill men and built the sawmills'. The Forks census and deed suggest the move was really c.1800; daughter Susan was born at Nanticoke (WikiTree: Shickshinny) in May 1800. A captive's 1833 narrative says Indians killed Asa Upson on 28 Mar 1780 at 'Stewart's Flats, now owned by Frederick Croup, in Plymouth', and the 'Dutch Fishery' shad haul below Nanticoke used 'the upper end of the Croup farm' as its landing (confirmed that a Frederick Croup owned it by 1833; probable it is this man). His brother Philip's 1812 will named 'my dear brother Frederick Grupe' co-executor (Luzerne Will Book A p.128). Judge Thomas Cooper (1806-1811) jailed 'a gentleman named Croup' and Kingston constable Stephen Hollister for whispering in court - one of the charges that led to Cooper's removal in 1811; which Croup is unknown (speculative). The Croop mills and later Croop's Glen amusement park descend from his nephew John Croop's line, not his; Frederick was a farmer and landowner near the river. He married Mary Young ('Frederick and Mary (Young) Croup', Harvey Book p.354). Known children: Susan (1800-1863, m. Philip Shupp Jr.) and Elizabeth (1802-1895, m. James Pringle). An unverified Ancestry list (WikiTree Grub-81) gives Sarah, Elizabeth, Mary, Margaret, Catherine, William, Peter and Ann (omitting Susan); FamilySearch gives Susan, John, Peter, Mary, Margaret, Catherine, Ann and William. Both he and Mary are said to have died in 1841; no record of the deaths was found online.

Frederick appears in the 1820 census of Plymouth as 'Frederick Crapp' (an indexing of Croup), with a large family including two young men, two girls aged 10-15 and a young woman ([R4-S1]); Elizabeth (b. c.1802) and her sisters fit those columns. In 1840 'Fred'k Croup' was still in Plymouth Township, a man in his seventies with a wife in her sixties and a younger couple, probably a married child, living with them ([R4-S2]). His will is in the county index as 'Croup, Frederick, Plymouth Twp., 1841', recorded in Will Book B at page 80 ([R4-S3]); the FamilySearch tree dates his death to before 10 April 1841 ([R4-S4]). The will itself has not been transcribed online; it should name his children, including Elizabeth Pringle and Susan Shupp.
